chapter_theme: Craving is the seed of all birth and the sorrow of sorrows, and its removal, not any other act, is the direct cause of an unchanging state. The whole section on renunciation ends here, by locating release at the moment when wanting stops.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: desire as the seed of birth (361), the excellence of not wanting (362-363), how release comes about (364), its praise from both sides (365), desire's danger (366), the benefit of cutting it (367), desire as the cause of sorrow (368), joy in this life (369), and what release is (370). Manakkudavar notes at 370 that the section on renunciation ends here.

361.reading: They say craving is the seed that, for all beings at all times, produces unceasing birth.
361.nuance: என்ப, 'they say', is read by Parimelazhagar as marking agreement among all schools. He supplies a mechanism: at death, craving carries the life to its next state. Kalaignar keeps the seed but removes birth.

362.reading: If you must want, want not to be born; that comes when you want not to want.
362.nuance: A paradox as neat as 350. The verb வேண்டு occurs in every clause, and the verse doesn't pretend desire can simply be stopped. It redirects desire until it undoes itself.

positions.position: Non-birth comes of itself to one who wants to want nothing.
positions.quote: அப்பிறவாமைதான் ஒரு பொருளையும் அவாவாமையை வேண்ட அவனுக்குத் தானே உண்டாம்.

positions.position: It is a warning: the misery that makes one wish one had never been born comes if desires aren't eliminated.

363.reading: There is no fine wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either.
363.nuance: It is pointed to name wanting nothing as wealth. Parimelazhagar explains why it is the top: human and divine wealth always have something above them, so only not wanting has no superior.

364.reading: Purity is the absence of craving, and that comes by wanting வாய்மை.
364.nuance: The word தூய்மை also differs: for Parimelazhagar it is release itself, as the soul's stains are gone, and for Manakkudavar it is the removal of defilement.

positions.position: வாய்மை here stands for the Supreme, who has truth, and wanting it means continuous contemplation.
வாய்மை means speaking truth, and those who speak truth come to have no desire.
positions.quote: அவ்வாசை யின்மை மெய் சொல்லுதலை விரும்ப வரும்,

365.reading: Those called 'freed' are those freed of craving; the rest are not so freed.
365.nuance: அற்றார் is left without an object, and that is the wit. Being cut free of other things is a partial matter, which Parimelazhagar makes explicit: others have only avoided some pains.

366.reading: It is virtue alone to fear; what deceives a person is craving.
366.nuance: Craving is a confidence trick: Manakkudavar has it stand in front like a benefactor and then lead one down. Parimelazhagar has it slip in through a moment's inattention, even for someone close to release. So vigilance has no end point.

positions.position: It deceives by acting first as a friend.
positions.quote: வஞ்சனை செய்தல் - நன்றி செய்வாரைப் போல முன்னே நின்று , பின்னே தீக்கதியுள் உய்த்தல்.

367.reading: If one cuts off craving thoroughly, the deeds that don't fail come in the way one wishes.
367.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a bold antinomian comment: once craving is fully cut, no other virtue need be done, and everything one does is virtue. The verse says only that the right deeds arrive.

368.reading: Those without craving have no sorrow; if it exists, sorrow keeps coming, unfailing, on and on.
368.nuance: The claim seems too simple, since those without craving still get sick. Parimelazhagar sees this and limits it: the suffering that came with the body is already earned, and the verse means suffering created now.

369.reading: Joy will be unbroken ஈண்டும், if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes.
369.nuance: Craving is not just the cause of sorrow but is itself the worst sorrow. Parimelazhagar explains that it hurts both at its source and in its fruit.

positions.position: ஈண்டும் means 'even here', so joy comes while still in the body.
positions.quote: அவன் வீடு பெற்ற வழியே அன்றி உடம்போடு நின்ற வழியும் இன்பம் இடையறாது.

positions.position: ஈண்டும் means 'it swells', so joy increases without break, and Parimelazhagar notes this view.

370.reading: If one gives up craving, whose nature is never to be filled, right then it gives a nature that never shifts.
370.nuance: The rhyme of ஆரா and பேரா sets an insatiable nature against an immovable one, and அந்நிலையே makes it immediate. Parimelazhagar calls this person liberated while living and quotes the Tiruvaymoli. The verse says only that the nature doesn't move.

links.note: Both solve the same problem by the same paradox: you can't leave desire by force, so desire is used against itself. 350 holds to the one without holding, and 362 wants to be without wanting.

விழுச்செல்வம் names not wanting here and learning in 400. Taken with 241 and 411, the Kural has awarded the title of true wealth to at least four things, and that suggests the phrase is a rhetorical form and not a doctrine.

298 says inner purity comes through truth. 364 gives the missing link: purity is the absence of craving, and wanting truth brings it. On Parimelazhagar's view, the meaning of truth has shifted from speech to the Supreme.

351 traces birth to confusion and 361 traces it to craving, and both claim to be the root. Parimelazhagar makes them a sequence, with ignorance first and craving following, but the verses each say it singly.
Virtue as a kind of fear: in 201 the excellent fear evil deeds, and in 366 what is to be feared is craving, which is behind those deeds. It is the same moral fear moved one step closer to its source.

320 says all pain rests on those who caused pain, and 368 says sorrow comes from craving and doesn't come to those without it. Two single-source explanations of suffering, one ethical and one psychological, sit a few chapters apart.

Just ten verses apart, this one ends the section on renunciation by promising a nature that can't be shifted, once craving goes. 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first. The Kural moves from the highest claim for human release straight to the strongest claim against human power.
அற்றார் are the destitute in 226, to be fed, and the freed in 365, to be revered. The same word for lacking marks both the most pitiable person and the most complete one.

source_issues: 361, 363, 365: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
366: Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint அவர் for அவா (கெடுக்கவல்லது அவர்).
